messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] source of n_eff in Matt trick?
parts:
Hmm, this is disturbing.  We should figure out what is going on here.
A

On Jun 9, 2013, at 8:59 AM, Adam Slez wrote:

Bob, Ben, and Andrew,

I redid the analysis used to produce the previous speed tests which, I forgot to mention, were only based on 2K iterations (hence why some of the R-hats were so high).  Here's what is going on in the setup of the new tests:

1.  I used 4 chains with 10K iterations.

2.  I estimated three additional models.  As per Bob's suggestion, the first uses the Matt trick as before, but initial values are set to zero.  The second uses the Matt trick, but the x variable has been mean centered via the use of a transformed data block.  The third model also uses a mean-centered x, but does not use the Matt trick.

3.  Output was produced using the monitor command so as to ensure comparability between Stan and JAGS, as per the discussion here.  This speaks to Bob's question regarding the calculation of effective sample size.  One thing I noticed is that the monitor results did not match the print results.  I might expect this when looking at the JAGS output, but this also happened in Stan as well.  My understanding is that the print output in Stan is based on the summary function.  How do the summary calculations differ from the monitor calculations?

Here's my reading of the findings:

1.  JAGS outpaces Stan by quite a bit, regardless of how the model is specified in Stan.

2.  Stan models which use the Matt trick seem to do worse than Stan models without the Matt trick.

3.  Models with and without the Matt trick differ in terms of which parameters they are able to efficiently estimate.  Models with the Matt trick do better with respect to bx as compared to u0 or sigma.  The opposite holds for models without the Matt trick.

4.  Mean centering doesn't seem to help much.

5.  To speak to Bob's earlier question, in terms of posterior variance Stan actually seems to be doing slightly better when we look at the standard deviation.  Things are obviously a bit different when we look at, say, the standard error of the mean which corrects for effective sample size. Overall, JAGS seems to be doing better here, in large part because of the fact that Stan does well with either u0 and sigma or bx, but not both.  More specifically, we see Stan without the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with to the standard error of the mean for u0 and sigma.  In contrast, if we either center x or set initial values to 0, we see Stan with the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with respect to the standard error of the mean for bx.

I have also attached the diagnostics requested by Bob and Ben.  These include both a traceplot for u0, sigma, and bx, as well as the pairs graph depicting chain-specific results (chains 1 and 2 are on the first page, while chains 3 and 4 are on the second).  To show the correlation between parameter estimates, I have also included a scatterplot matrix depicting draws for u0, sigma, bx, and five randomly chosen group effects (both transformed and untransformed). I'm not sure whether this is the best approach for answering Bob's question as to whether the traceplots show high correlation of the u0, sigma, and e_u variables.  In the first place, I'm not sure that what I did even counts as a traceplot in the usual sense. It would also be preferable to look at all of the u and e_u terms, but I couldn't think of a good way to do this given that I have 144 groups and, hence, 288 + 3 = 291 parameters to graph.  All graphs correspond to the row in the table labeled "Stan w/Matt" (i.e. I used the Matt trick but did not center x or force initial values to 0).

My read is that the chains for u0 and sigma aren't mixing especially well (at least not compared to bx) and that there is some correlation between sigma, u, and e_u, though maybe not a crazy amount.  The u terms seem okay, there is some evidence of correlation between sigma and the e_u terms, and there is definitely correlation among the e_u terms themselves.  Again, this approach is less than perfect because I'm only looking at a handful of u/e_u terms.  Things could be worse elsewhere in the model.

Adam

On Friday, June 7, 2013 11:29:26 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
On Friday, June 7, 2013 10:39:53 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'm curious about what's going on here conceptually.

With the Matt trick, you sample

   e_u ~ normal(0,1)

and then set:

   u <- u0 + sigma * e_u

u0, sigma, and e_u all have low n_eff (< 70)
whereas u has a high n_eff (2,000).

Is it the extra variability of the three variables combined
that gives u relatively low autocorrelation?

This is odd. I would be interested to see the joint distribution of u0 and sigma, which can be done via rstan with something like

pairs(model2, pars = c("u0", "sigma"), chain_id = c(1,2))

in this case the results for chain 1 will be in the lower triangle and chain 2 will be in the upper triangle. I would bet at least one of the chains is messed up.

Ben
